summary:
Ignopticon is a free, open wildfire map at ignopticon.earth, built by the Babylonian Belugas for NASA Space Apps 2026. 

We have three pages. Fire watch shows each active fire's NASA FEDS perimeter, VIIRS hotspots, wind and containment, with a slider that steps a 12-hour ELMFIRE forecast through its most likely and worst cases. History offers a burning calendar, comparisons with past years and the FIRMS archive. Technical documents every method and score.

For crews, radio and phone dead zones are modelled with SPLAT! on terrain, using FCC cell towers and repeaters the crew adds themselves. Routes over OpenStreetMap roads avoid the active edge and limit time out of contact, and all of it is cached on the device, so it works without signal.

Researchers can reproduce everything. The code, modelling log, scoring scripts and frozen fire lists are open on GitHub, and the harmonized grids and forecasts are served as plain files.

On held-out fires, ELMFIRE located about a third more growth than simple rules across 97 fire-days, and it beat the operational PyreCast forecast on 25 of 33. The forecasts don't model firefighting, only how the fire would spread unchecked.
details:
Ignopticon is a free, open wildfire map at ignopticon.earth. It brings together three things that usually live in separate places: consistent long-term fire history, a short-range spread forecast for every active fire, and practical information for crews on the ground.

It starts with the challenge itself. MODIS has observed fire since 2000 at about 1 km resolution, while VIIRS, from 2012, sees at 375 m and detects far more fire. Joined naively, the record shows US fire activity falling sharply in 2012, which is the sensor change, not the fire. We built a daily 0.1-degree grid of the US from four MODIS and VIIRS products and trained a gradient-boosting model to estimate, for every MODIS-era day and place, the probability that VIIRS would have seen fire. On that harmonized record the false drop and the false downward trend disappear, so this week's fire activity can be compared fairly with any week since 2003.

For each active fire, the site shows the NASA FEDS perimeter, VIIRS hotspots, wind, containment and the population nearby. It runs the ELMFIRE fire-spread model for 12 hours from the observed perimeter, with high-resolution weather and fuel maps. It gives a most likely case and a worst case built from 11 weather variants, sized to catch about 80% of growth, having been run on UW's Tillicum Supercomputer over credits we submitted a request to loan.

For crews, it maps radio and phone dead zones with the SPLAT! terrain propagation model and suggests routes that avoid the active edge while staying in contact, and it all works offline once loaded.

We hope our tool is trustworthy and reliable. Operational tools exist, but few publish how well they do for research verification and to the general public. We tested every forecast on fires chosen before the model ran. Across 97 fire-days, ELMFIRE located about a third more of the next 12 hours of growth than simple distance or wind rules. Against the operational PyreCast forecast on the same fires, ours did better on 25 of 33 fire-days. We intend Ignopticon to give communities, crews and researchers a free tool whose accuracy anyone can check, along with honest context on whether a fire season is unusual.

Our team weighed several factors: honesty about uncertainty, testing only on fires that were still spreading, and the fact that the forecasts show spread without firefighting.

We also worked to support crews working without signal, and especially about keeping everything free and open.
